Key cues are the yellow-diamond priority road sign with a white border, the red-and-white diagonal hazard marker on the traffic island, and the blue circular “keep right” sign. This exact combination—especially the yellow diamond (DE Sign 306) and the style of galvanized signal poles and signal heads with a small green right-turn arrow—is strongly characteristic of Germany (also seen in Austria/Switzerland, but less commonly with this exact street furniture mix). Additionally, text visible on a billboard appears to be German (“Gemeinsam …”), reinforcing Germany over neighboring countries.
City-level: The broad, tree-lined urban arterial with separated sidewalk/cycle facilities, the grey modular curb stones, and the Munich-style traffic signal heads and bollards are consistent with large southern German cities. The overall look (dense greenery, light-grey pavers, and pole-mounted priority sign directly above a signal head) aligns well with footage commonly seen in Munich compared to Frankfurt or Hamburg, though this is not uniquely identifying.
Street-level: Specific to this junction are: a side street posted as one-way with a no‑entry sign, a priority-road sign mounted on the main corner signal pole, a right-turn arrow traffic light, a small refuge with a blue “keep right” sign and a red‑white hazard marker, and multiple cycle-route signs on slim posts along the right sidewalk. These elements together define the immediate intersection but are not singular enough to pinpoint an exact street without readable street names.
Overall, the evidence supports Germany, likely Munich, but the precise street is uncertain.
